utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-98-29/1-PT, the Prosecutor versus Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We'd like to have the appearances, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Good morning. For the Prosecution, I'm Chester Stamp. Appearing with me is Mr. Manoj Sachdeva, and our case manager is Ms. Biljana Blazevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. May I have the appearances on the side of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning. I am Branislav Tapuskovic, attorney-at-law from Belgrade, and I represent the Defence of the accused, Dragomir Milosevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to greet all those present here, the representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence counsel. I would like also to greet General Dragomir Milosevic, who is here in this courtroom. According to the Rules, this Status Conference has to take place every 120 days. As you know, the last Status Conference took place in October this year, on the 12th of October, 2005. Therefore, I thought that it was necessary to have another Status Conference in order to see what was the status of exchanges of documents and to raise a number of issues. First of all, the reason why we have this hearing this morning at 8.00 a.m. is that we currently have at the Tribunal only two courtrooms available, Courtroom I and Courtroom III, because Courtroom II is currently being renovated. As a result, we have to hold hearings at a very early time in the day in order to be able to deal with a number of cases at the pre-trial stage. The other issue I would like to stress is the following. As you know, through an order I issued, I asked the Prosecution to send me, at the latest, on the 20th of January, 2006, the final version of its pre-trial brief as well as the list of witnesses and exhibits, in order to allow me - and I will do that later on - in order to allow me to ask the Defence to file their pre-trial brief in accordance with the Rules 65 ter (F), to file their brief. And once this has been done, I will draw up a report for the Chamber, for the President of Trial Chamber II to refer the matter to the President of the Tribunal in order for the President to assign Judges to try this case. At this point in time, I am completely unable to tell you when the trial will start because it will all depend on what courtrooms will be available. It will also depend on what Judges will be available. And at this point in time, I do not have any information that would allow me to tell you when the trial will start in this case. This is unfortunate. This is also contrary to the interest of the accused, who's been waiting for his trial to start for about a year. It would of course be better if the parties could have information about when the trial will start. As a Judge, I'm completely -- I do not -- I cannot -- I do not have any control over this because I cannot, myself, set the date of the beginning of the trial, contrary to what happens in other jurisdictions. Now let me move on to the issues of disclosure. During the last Status Conference, if I remember correctly, there were still a number of issues unresolved regarding disclosure under Rule 68 -- 66(A)(ii) regarding witness statements. I hope this has been resolved. I'm now going to turn to Mr. Stamp. Could you please tell me regarding disclosure under Rules 68 to 66 -- 68 and 66, if disclosure is taking place as it should.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Disclosure is taking place within the confines that our resources permit in respect of Rule 68. We have disclosed as the Rules provide all material which we know to fall under Rule 68; that is material tending to be potentially exculpatory. And in addition to that, we are conducting searches for material which may also be potentially exculpatory on Rule 68. We have received recently from the Defence counsel additional criteria, that is additional search terms or guidance, as to the areas that we should search in our -- in the evidence collections that we have for material which might assist the Defence and we are doing so. The department of the OTP that is responsible for that has taken on the matter; they are conducting the searches. And when the results are in, we will have to review them and disclose the material relevant. In respect to Rule 66(A)(ii), that is the statement of witnesses, we had in our first disclosure, that is a disclosure of the confirmation material, disclosed -- I cannot recall the precise number, but a quantity of witness statements, both in English, the language that they were taken in, and the language of the accused. There has been further disclosure of witness statements in English. When we comply, as we intend to, with the court orders in respect to the witness list, that is when we have determined, having contacted, witnesses having settled issues of protective measures, and a variety of issues we will have to settle in determining our witness list under Rule 65, we will deliver all the additional witness statements along with copies in B/C/S, that is along with copies in a language of the accused. So we are up-to-date with all the disclosure in accordance with the Rules and in accordance with orders hat the Court has issued. And we intend to and we are trying to go a little bit further in that, in that we are also trying to disclose to the Defence translations of material that we disclose under Rule 66(B) and Rule 68, which is not really required by the Rules, but we are attempting to do so nonetheless. Unless there are any further questions, I think I will close with that for the moment, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Before I give the floor to the Defence on that matter, let me say that as far as I'm concerned, following what I've heard, I understand that you've said that it's not required by the Rules. But as a Judge, it seems to me that the Statute of the International Tribunal, when relating to the rights of the accused, makes it an obligation for the Prosecution to provide to the accused in a language that he understands all documents against him and also all documents of an exculpatory nature. That's stated and provided for by the Statute of the Tribunal. Let me now give the floor to the Defence for any comments they would like to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. What you said at the end is precisely an important issue outstanding for the Defence. According to your decision and the deadline you set by which the Prosecutor should fulfil what is provided for in Rule 65 ter (E), among other things, under Rule 65 ter it provides for what is contained under point (ii) of that Rule, 65 ter (E)(ii), where it is stated, first of all, that the name and pseudonym of each witness must be provided and a summary of the facts on which each witness will testify. Now, if we link that up with what Rule 66 provides, that is to say before the summaries are provided of the witness statements within the deadline Your Honour has set, the Prosecutor should present to the Defence all the statements in their entirety of possible witnesses to be called in the trial against Dragomir Milosevic. And now this is where we come across a problem which makes our work in preparation of the Defence case more difficult. Pursuant to Rule 66(A), as you know full well, the Prosecutor is duty-bound to place everything he has at the disposal of the Defence team in a language the accused understands. And in the spirit of Rule 66(A)(i), we have a list of witnesses that could come under Rule 66(A)(ii). However, we received a list of 64 witnesses. However, it was stated that they are possible witnesses pursuant to Rule 66(B) or Rule 68. So they can be used either as evidence for the Prosecution pursuant to Rule 66(B) or pursuant to Rule 68. So they did not state whether -- which rule they would come under. And the most important point which Mr. Stamp raised: It has not been provided in a language that the accused understands. So strictly speaking, pursuant to Rule 66(A)(ii), as provided by that provision, we have not received up to the present date what we should have received for us to be able to function properly. And for me to receive instructions from the accused that he has read the material because it is not sufficient if I tell him what I noted on the basis of reading the documents, but that I should be given instructions from him on the spirit of his Defence case. Therefore, at this point in time this is a very significant problem and makes life for the Defence team much more difficult, and I fear that that might be one of the reasons for I will have to ask for a postponement, a time given to me to respond to the Prosecution pre-trial brief to file my own brief and response. So at this point in time that is a problem. And I was told by Mr. Stamp yesterday at the meeting we had, and his associates, that I could count on a promise to let me have the statements in translation, that is to say in a language understood by the accused, very soon. But, as I say, this is an impediment in my communication with the accused and the instruction of feedback from the accused that I could receive in order to prepare his defence trial as efficaciously as possible. So at this point in time, that is the outstanding problem that we face for my job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. So I take note of the fact that several months later -- because we raised that issue for the first time on the 12th of October. We raised the issue of Rule 66(A)(ii) at that time already. I do not understand why the Prosecution, who is considering calling a number of witnesses, I do not understand why the Prosecution has not disclosed these documents to the Defence. And I understand it even less, because as the Defence counsel has underlined it, the accused is entitled to know what charges have been brought against him, he is entitled to study these documents in his cell and to give instructions to his counsel. That's the way things go in every jurisdiction in the world. Therefore, I've come -- I come to the conclusion that the Prosecution has not disclosed a number of documents translated in the language of the accused. Let me remind you, Mr. Stamp, that penalties are provided for in the Rules if the Prosecution does not fulfil its obligations. Because when a party wastes time, this time can never be recuperated, made up for. And let me remind you that the accused is presumed innocent. He's been in detention for a year. And the least he can expect, the least he's entitled to, is to know what sort of material will be used at trial against him. What can you tell us about this, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I repeat with emphasis and with respect, Your Honour. The Prosecution is in compliance with all our disclosure obligations under the Rules and pursuant to the orders of the Court. The issue in respect to a variety of statements and material that we have disclosed pursuant to Rule 66(B) and Rule 66(A) is whether or not some of the material has been translated into the language of the accused. The -- the -- this Tribunal and the jurisprudence of this Tribunal in many cases has made it absolutely clear that there is no obligation on the Prosecution to translate documents or statements disclosed under those Rules, and there are many cases in which -- in which that decision has been made. And I speak about disclosure under Rule 66(B) and Rule 68. We, however, have only taken and will insofar as translations are available disclose to the Defence translations of those documents. The second area is the area of Rule 66(A)(ii), disclosure, that is disclosure of witness statements. As I indicated, many, if not most, of the witness statements have been disclosed to the Defence when the confirmation material was served on the Defence. However, the Rules provide for the Prosecution to disclose all of those statements at a time to be set by the Pre-Trial Judge. The Court has set that time, and that time is the 20th of January. In the interim, the Prosecution is on an obligation to do a variety of things, some of which are indicated to this Court, in preparation of its witness list. Witnesses -- documents need to be reviewed, and without going into the details of it, there are a huge amount of work the Prosecution must overcome to prepare and present a witness list. The Rule provides, Rule 66(A)(ii), that the Prosecution shall make available to the Defence in a language which the accused understands, (ii), within the time-limit prescribed by the Trial Chamber or the Pre-Trial Judge the statements of all witnesses who the Prosecution intends to call. That time-limit has been set at the 20th of January. We, subject to an application I intend to make shortly, intend to do so and to comply with that order. In respect to all the other areas of disclosure, we have disclosed all the material, numerous documents, as early as they were available. We insist, with respect, Your Honour, that we are not obligated under the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, as decided in many cases, to translate all of the numerous, countless, documents that will come up in these various searches and which are to be disclosed to the Defence. However, we will do so when translations are available. And having regard to our amicable discussions so far with the Defence, those 64 documents in which they've expressed an interest, where translations are available, we will give them to the Defence. And we intend to continue to comply with all our obligations under the Rules and as ordered by the Court. May it please you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Let me give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An additional explanation; perhaps I omitted to say that a moment ago. As Defence counsel for the accused, Dragomir Milosevic, I did not insist on the fact that the Prosecution should disclose all the materials they have at their disposal, and, among other things, evidence pursuant to Rule 68 in translation. In a letter and yesterday in talking to the Prosecutors, I set forward my views, my position, that there is no reason why what the Prosecution has in translation should be supplied to us. However, the problem that we're facing now -- if we look at Rule 65 ter (E)(ii)(a) and (b) provides, and it says here that the time-limit for filing is the 20th of January, as it says in that Rule (E)(ii)(b), a succinct summary of the facts that a witness is to testify about, whereas Rule 66 says that a copy of the statements of all witnesses in complete form, that is the fundamental difference. What this Court has been ordered should be done by the 20th of January does not include what Rule 66(A)(ii) states. We have to have those complete statements. Now, whether they're all going to be used or not is another matter, but that is the fundamental difference. So it is not the Prosecution that is duty-bound pursuant to a ruling by you to provide us with statements but a summary of statements with respect to the material facts. And Rule 66(A)(ii) speaks about something quite different. We already have had to have those statements, and there a deadline should also be set which relates to a time before the 20th, by which time we should be provided with those statements definitively. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I take note of this issue, and I will very soon release an order about this. But let me say already that it is certain that when the Prosecutor considers calling a witness at trial, the statement of that particular witness has to be disclosed to the Defence in the language of the accused. This is a cardinal rule, a fundamental rule. In order to dispel any confusion, any doubt, let me tell you that tomorrow I will issue a new order related to the issue of material and witness lists that you will have to provide me. You will receive a very detailed order tomorrow about that issue, and the time-limit is the 20th of January. I find this a very important issue, because when I -- I'd like to refer you to the Galic case. In the Galic case, 171 witnesses were called, 16 expert witnesses testified, 1600 exhibits for the Defence, and 650 for the Prosecution, plus a number of exhibits from the Chamber, 14. And since these -- the facts dealt here are included in the Galic case, we can logically deduct that a number of witnesses called in the Galic case will be called in this case or referred to in this case. Let me remind you that the Galic case lasted 223 days. The Prosecution submitted its case over 127 days and the Defence 96 days. That was the duration of Defence case. Therefore, this case is going to be a very lengthy one, and we have to have a proper preparation for this case. And that's the reason why I'm going to send you that order. I find it totally unacceptable that one year on we still have discussions on whether or not the accused has received in a language that he understands a number of materials -- material or documents. That's totally unacceptable. I'm going to issue an order in order to specify and stress all these points. Let me also say the following to the Prosecution. I see that there are two of you here today. In the Galic case there were five members in the Prosecution team. I do not know what the Prosecution intends in terms of the number of trial attorneys in this particular case. But let me point out the following legal issue. In the Galic case, the Articles 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute were referred to. In the Galic judgement, the issue of Article 7(1) was not considered or was rejected by the Chamber because Galic was found guilty under Article 7(3) of the Statute --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 7(1) of the Statute and Article 7(3) was not dealt with. Therefore, if you want to invoke Articles 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute in this particular case, in your pre-trial brief you will have to outline very clearly what elements are relevant to Article 7.3. And in the list of witnesses, in the list of materials - but I will specify that in the order tomorrow - you will have to specify very clearly what sort of exhibits are related to Article 7(3) and what witnesses will be called in relation to Article 7(3) in order to avoid any type of confusion in the trial later on. This does cause a certain confusion because 7.1, 7.3 are sometimes contradictory. The Chambers don't take into consideration the 7(3), whereas it is included in the indictment. Let me remind the Prosecution, the Prosecution is fully aware of this, that in the decision rendered in the Galic case, a decision was rendered on a majority basis. 7(3) was discarded, whereas the dissenting opinion from one of the Judges clearly mentioned 7(3). This will have to be spelled out in your pre-trial brief. I will now speed things up a little bit, because as you know a trial is starting in this courtroom at 9.00. There is another point I wish to address, i.e., the computer used by General Milosevic. I had addressed the registry on this particular matter. The registry responded by saying that some accused had received computers from their families, but for security reasons an order had been rendered whereby the accused were not entitled to use these computers. One needed to check whether on the memory cards of these computers that some information that could perhaps not be acceptable to the Detention Unit, and which they are [as interpreted]. So the Registrar told me that all the accused in detention would be entitled to use a personal computer. I don't know whether this has been done or not. Now, the Defence counsel, do you have anything to say relating to this particular matter, i.e., the fact that the accused can use a personal computer?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, we will not be opposing that decision; he understands what is at stake. However, as far as I know he still has no PC in his cell to use. A promise was made that everybody there would be given one, in view of the new system that will be used. However, I talked to my client yesterday, and he still doesn't have a PC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General, would you stand up, please. Would you like to say something on any particular matter? You have the floor. If you wish to address me, you may, and you can talk about any issue you would like to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour, for allowing me to say what I wish to say. First of all, I would like to thank you yet again. I wish to point out that had I not been the accused in question, the discussion between the OTP and the Defence might have provided some significant points of interest. I do understand the points raised by both sides, nevertheless the circumstances that led to the filing of the indictment against me were such that lots of different things were done, all sorts of things. The OTP may now find themselves in a difficult situation gathering all the evidence that they believe they need, but that is ultimately no concern of mine. If I am to face this uncertainty, which I seem to be, I cannot help but wonder why my request was thrown out to be provisionally released. I do not believe that this was a just decision, and I believe that I have been prejudiced by that decision. However, I am here. I am prepared to follow and accept everything that goes on. There are a number of things that do not depend on me, but rather on the people under whose jurisdiction I now stand. That is all I have to say on the subject. As for the PC, everything is now clear and resolved. We can no longer use the PCs that we obtained through personal channels. We shall probably be given other equipment to use. When exactly is something that only the registry can decide. That is all I have to say on these matters. In case there are any other questions that Your Honour wishes to raise with me, please do so. I have no other special issues to raise. I must reiterate, though, that there is no way I can prepare for my trial if I do not start receiving documents in a language I understand, or documents in their entirety, so that I can have a full view of what they are about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your comments. Under our Rules, there are two questions I need to ask you. The first one relates to your detention conditions. Are your conditions good or are you -- do you have any complaints to file?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for asking, Your Honour. It is true that this is a crucial issue to the life of all those living in detention. I must say I really have no objections, although the question itself seems to be addressed in a slightly official way. If I were in a different environment, I could, perhaps, raise a point or two; but for that I would need to talk to the people involved and not raise general issues here in court. My conclusion has to be, however, that I have no serious objections that have a negative bearing on my life in detention. Thank you. That's as much as I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another mandatory question relates to your state of health. Do you have any health problems or is everything all right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As people say where I come from, touch wood. No problems so far, thank you. Thank you for asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. You may sit down, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me turn to the Defence counsel. The Prosecution will file the documents by the 20th of January, a list of witnesses, pre-trial brief, as well as all the requisite material pursuant to Rule 65 ter. Following the filing of this material by the 20th of January, 2006, the Defence team will have one month to file its comments. So the Defence will have to respond by the 20th of February, 2006. If they have any comments to make. Mr. Stamp, do you have any comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I move quite quickly, Your Honour. The Prosecution fully agrees with the sentiments expressed about all the material to be used in the case against the accused being received by him in a language which he understands. He has received much of that material already, and we will ensure that all of the material is delivered to the accused in that manner. And I am also grateful for the guidance in respect to the pre-trial brief and the precision with which we must express ourselves in respect of Rule 7(3). There is one additional matter. I had discussed it with my friend, and he indicated he would not object. Having regard to his travel, his travel schedules, I understand that he intends to be here next at the end of January, and having regard to our schedules as well within the Prosecution, I was wondering -- and it's a matter entirely for the Court, and I don't think the Defence would be prejudiced, if the time for us to deliver all of the material, that is all of the exhibits translated in a language that the accused understands, all of the statements translated into a language that he understands, as well as the pre-trial brief, and the witness and the exhibit lists linked to the witnesses as ordered by the Court, I am wondering if that time could be extended to the 31st of January, that is the end of the month. It will not, it is submitted, do any prejudice to the Defence, as counsel would be returning here on that day and we could hand everything over in one large batch and give guidance as to what the material is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I agree with your proposal. These -- this material will be handed over by the 31st of January, which means that all of this will be delayed or postponed by a week, and the Defence will therefore file all of its comments before the 28th of February. So you will have an additional week, and the deadline has now been set for the 28th of February. Does the Defence counsel -- before we adjourn this hearing, would the Defence counsel have any comments to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further points to raise or comments to make. All these matters were discussed yesterday at our meeting, and it was within the same framework that I understood the proposal of the OTP. Also in relation to my travel, usually I'm only able to travel once a month. The Registry should have some understanding for the fact that I have to travel on multiple occasions over the next month. There has been a strict allocation of one time a month only. In January, I will have to be here twice at least, early in January, and at the time that I am bound to be receiving what has been mentioned by the OTP. I think that is the way it should be, and that will make my job a great deal easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we have addressed all the items on the agenda for today. I thank you all for having attended this hearing. We will not have an opportunity to see each other before the end of the year, so I would like to wish you a happy new year, and I hope that in the year 2006 both parties will enjoy very satisfactory professional relations, and we hope that this trial can unfold in the best conditions possible. I'd like to thank you.
